solutions.text: PHẦN A: 1. Some conditions, such as certain heart problems, are HEREDITARY and tend to run in families across several generations. — "Hereditary" (tính từ) nghĩa là di truyền qua gen; thường đi với "disorders/disease/traits", khác với "inherited" mang nghĩa rộng hơn. 2. Doctors are increasingly able to identify a genetic PREDISPOSITION towards particular illnesses long before any symptoms appear. — "Predisposition" cần giới từ "to/towards" đi kèm ("predisposition to/towards a disease"), không dùng "for". 3. A single genetic MUTATION in one gene can be enough to trigger a serious inherited disorder. — "Mutation" là danh từ đếm được chỉ sự thay đổi trong DNA; động từ tương ứng là "mutate", không dùng "mutation" như động từ. 4. Under laboratory conditions, scientists can observe how quickly a virus is able to REPLICATE itself inside a host cell. — "Replicate" nghĩa là tự sao chép chính xác; dễ nhầm với "replace" (thay thế) nên cần chú ý phát âm và nghĩa. 5. Genetic engineers have developed wheat varieties that are more RESISTANT to drought and disease than earlier strains. — "Resistant" luôn đi với giới từ "to" ("resistant to drought/pests"), không dùng "against" hay "from". 6. Height is a physical TRAIT that is influenced by both genetic factors and childhood nutrition. — "Trait" là đặc điểm/đặc tính di truyền hoặc tính cách; thường đi với "genetic trait", "inherit a trait". 7. Hospitals in several countries now offer GENE EDITING as an experimental treatment for a small number of rare inherited conditions. — "Gene editing" viết rời khi là danh từ độc lập; chỉ thêm gạch nối khi làm tính từ ghép trước danh từ ("gene-editing technology"). 8. Many people confuse reproductive CLONING with therapeutic cloning, even though the two processes serve very different purposes. — "Cloning" là quá trình tạo ra sinh vật giống hệt về gen; cần phân biệt "reproductive cloning" và "therapeutic cloning". 9. Genetic MODIFICATION of crops is often defended on the grounds that it can improve resistance to pests. — "Modification" là danh từ chỉ sự biến đổi; viết tắt "GM" chỉ dùng cho tính từ (genetically modified), không thay thế danh từ này. 10. Historians often note that the discredited theory of EUGENICS was used to justify deeply unethical policies in the twentieth century. — "Eugenics" là danh từ số ít không đếm được, mang hàm ý tiêu cực mạnh trong lịch sử nên cần dùng cẩn trọng. 11. Some scientists have called for a MORATORIUM on certain forms of experimental gene therapy until safety guidelines are agreed internationally. — "Moratorium" nghĩa là lệnh cấm/đình chỉ tạm thời; collocation phổ biến là "call for/impose a moratorium on". 12. Researchers are studying whether STEM CELL therapy could help regenerate tissue damaged by injury or disease. — "Stem cell" là danh từ ghép không cần gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ khác ("stem cell research/therapy").

PHẦN B: 1. Band 7: Scientists can genetically modify plants to make them more resistant to disease and drought. Band 8: Advances in gene editing have made it possible to engineer crop varieties that are markedly more resistant to disease and drought than their conventional counterparts. 2. Band 7: Hereditary illnesses can be passed down from parents to their children through genes. Band 8: Hereditary disorders, rooted in genetic predisposition, can increasingly be identified and, in some cases, managed before symptoms ever emerge. 3. Band 7: Many people are concerned about the ethics of human cloning. Band 8: The prospect of human cloning continues to provoke considerable bioethical debate, not least because of the profound questions it raises about identity and consent. 4. Band 7: Editing a baby's genes before birth raises difficult ethical questions. Band 8: Germline editing of embryos is arguably one of the most contentious issues in modern science, given that any changes made would be passed on to future generations. 5. Band 7: Genetic testing allows people to find out if they have a predisposition to certain diseases. Band 8: Were genetic testing to become more widely accessible, individuals could be alerted to a hereditary predisposition long before any clinical symptoms appear. 6. Band 7: Some governments have banned certain types of genetic experiments because of safety concerns. Band 8: In light of persistent safety concerns, several governments have imposed a moratorium on certain categories of genetic research pending further international guidance. 7. Band 7: Companies that collect genetic data need to protect it carefully and use it responsibly. Band 8: Given how sensitive genetic data is, companies that gather it arguably have a fiduciary duty to safeguard it and to be transparent about how it is used. 8. Band 7: New biotechnology could help increase food production and reduce hunger. Band 8: Not only could biotechnology bolster food security through more resilient, disease-resistant crops, but it may also, some researchers argue, ease pressure on land already strained by climate change.

passages.text: Two strands of contemporary genetics, related in principle but rarely discussed together, have begun to define what the public conversation about the field looks like. The first is heritable, or germline, editing — the deliberate alteration of eggs, sperm or embryos in ways that would be passed on to future generations. The second, far less prominent in public coverage, is pharmacogenomics, the use of an individual patient's genetic profile to guide the choice and dose of medicines they take. The two raise different ethical questions and operate on different timescales, but a careful reading of the recent literature suggests that the disagreements within each strand have begun to shape how the other is governed.

The germline debate took its current form after the 2018 announcement, by the Chinese researcher He Jiankui, that he had used CRISPR to edit the genomes of two embryos who were subsequently born. The experiment was widely condemned by the international scientific community, which judged that it had proceeded without adequate ethical review, sufficient safety data or meaningful informed consent. A 2019 statement signed by leading scientific academies in eighteen countries called for a moratorium on heritable human genome editing until clearer international standards could be agreed. Five years on, the moratorium has held in formal terms, but the underlying disagreement about whether, when and on whose authority such editing could ever be acceptable has not been resolved.

One important line of argument has been developed by the bioethicist Françoise Baylis, formerly of Dalhousie University. Baylis argues that heritable editing differs from somatic editing — which alters only the cells of a single patient — not merely in scientific consequence but in moral structure. Decisions made today would commit people not yet born to changes they cannot consent to, and would do so under conditions of significant remaining uncertainty about long-term effects. The standard procedural safeguards of medicine, in her view, are not designed for that intergenerational reach and cannot simply be extended to cover it. Baylis is careful to distinguish a moratorium from a permanent ban; her preferred position is a slow, broad, multi-jurisdictional deliberation in which patient advocacy groups, disability scholars and non-Western voices are explicitly heard.

A different emphasis is offered by the molecular biologist Jennifer Doudna of the University of California, Berkeley, who shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for her contribution to the development of CRISPR. Doudna has accepted the case for a moratorium on heritable clinical editing under current conditions, but she has resisted framings that treat the underlying science as inherently transgressive. The same enzymes, she points out, are being used to develop somatic therapies for sickle-cell disease, certain inherited blindnesses and several rare metabolic conditions; severing the two narratives risks both delaying defensible therapies and concealing how interconnected the laboratory work has become. Doudna's preferred regulatory framing is risk-tiered: stricter for heritable applications, more permissive for somatic therapies with clearly bounded effects.

These two positions are not in direct opposition, but they pull governance in different directions. If the priority is to prevent premature heritable interventions, the appropriate response is sustained moratoria and broad deliberation. If the priority is to keep somatic therapies on a workable timeline, the focus shifts to differential regulation, transparent clinical-trial registries and access policies for therapies that are extraordinarily expensive at launch.

The second strand, pharmacogenomics, has unfolded with less public drama but at considerable scale. According to a 2020 review in the journal Nature Reviews Genetics, more than two hundred and fifty medicines have been linked to specific genetic variants that affect either efficacy or risk of adverse reaction. Researchers including Munir Pirmohamed at the University of Liverpool have argued that integrating genotype testing into prescribing decisions can reduce adverse drug reactions, which on conservative estimates are responsible for several per cent of hospital admissions in high-income countries. Implementation has been slow but uneven: the Netherlands and several Scandinavian health systems have piloted pre-emptive panels in primary care, while most other systems still order tests reactively, usually after a treatment failure.

A third voice in the debate, from the geneticist Esteban Burchard of the University of California, San Francisco, has pointed out that pharmacogenomic evidence has been gathered disproportionately from populations of European ancestry. The implication is that recommendations derived from those datasets may apply unevenly to patients of African, Indigenous American or East Asian descent, particularly for medicines metabolised through genes that vary widely between populations. Burchard's argument is that fairness in pharmacogenomics — like fairness in algorithmic systems — depends crucially on the composition of the underlying dataset, and that current cohorts are not adequate to support universal recommendations.

Defenders of more cautious deployment have responded that the existing evidence, even with its gaps, already supports targeted use in well-characterised drug-gene pairs, and that waiting for fully representative cohorts would forgo demonstrable patient benefit. None of this disposes of Burchard's concern about ancestry imbalance, but it does suggest that the trade-offs between speed and representativeness are sharper than the language of equity sometimes implies.

Pull the two strands together and three sober predictions follow, each more cautious than enthusiasts or critics tend to offer. Heritable editing is unlikely, in the writer's view, to be approved for any non-research clinical use within the next decade. Somatic therapies are likely to keep expanding, with affordability rather than safety as their main near-term limit. And pharmacogenomic prescribing is likely to spread only incrementally, its pace set by whether health systems invest in genotype panels and whether cohorts grow more representative. The interesting question, taken together, is not whether genetic medicine will reshape clinical practice but on whose terms and in whose interest — and that, more than any further headline announcement, is the question on which the next decade of governance will be judged.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture extends our science-policy series — focusing on the empirical literature concerning the international governance of CRISPR-based gene-editing applications. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Magdalena Vrankovic — that's V-R-A-N-K-O-V-I-C, no accent on the C, no apostrophe. Vrankovic's 2018 monograph reframed gene-editing governance from a single-regulator licensing model into what she calls "tiered-oversight theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The cross-national survey I'll reference today was first conducted in 2017 — sorry, let me correct that, 2016; the published descriptive statistics in 2017 covered data collected in 2016. So whenever I refer to the baseline year, please record 2016. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Vrankovic's framework USED TO be operationalised using static rule-based licensing, NOW the field deploys mixed-methods designs incorporating expert-panel deliberation transcripts, and from 2027 a multi-jurisdictional consortium WILL be rolling out adaptive-pathway modules. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, mixed-methods deliberation analysis. Moving to terminology. The governance concept Vrankovic foregrounds — a layered regulatory architecture in which different categories of gene edit are routed to differently configured review bodies — is termed "tiered oversight". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: licensing scheme, regulatory pathway, approval protocol. All of these gesture toward overlapping mechanisms, but they are NOT interchangeable with Vrankovic's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is tiered oversight — t-i-e-r-e-d oversight. So when the older literature uses licensing scheme or approval protocol, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what bioethicists call the "edit-class continuum". When regulators describe how a gene-editing application is categorised for review, they sketch a graded continuum running from somatic therapeutic edits through somatic enhancement edits to heritable germline modifications. So, you know, you'll see researchers correcting a single mutation in a patient's blood cells to treat sickle-cell disease — that's somatic therapeutic. Or interventions intended to be passed to offspring — that's heritable germline. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the umbrella term. The umbrella term is the edit-class continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the survey data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the forty-seven jurisdictions we surveyed across five continents, MOST had codified some form of statutory restriction on heritable germline editing — roughly eighty-two per cent. Only a few — about six per cent — left germline editing entirely unregulated, and some — twelve per cent — relied on non-binding professional guidelines only. So statutory restriction dominates numerically, though the unregulated tail, though small, is theoretically significant for transnational research flows. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "regulatory drift". This refers to the phenomenon where statutes drafted before a technique matures fail to constrain emerging applications because their definitions were calibrated to an earlier technique generation. At the Riverside Bioethics Forum, our research team documented fifty-eight observable drift episodes across one biennial review cycle. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that stricter statutory language linearly produces stricter research practice is, frankly, not supported. Most of the jurisdictions in our survey did NOT exhibit the predicted monotonic alignment between statutory text and laboratory practice. Quite the opposite — many showed a wedge curve, with practice diverging from statute beyond a complexity threshold of around three regulator-defined edit subclasses. So the older "text-equals-practice" hypothesis, which predicts linear alignment, is empirically NOT corroborated by our survey. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT mixed-methods deliberation-analysis state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in today's seminar this afternoon. I want you to focus on the expert-panel transcript protocols specifically, not the adaptive-pathway futures or the legacy static rule-based licensing instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: gene-editing governance is tiered, not single-regulator; the technical term for layered regulatory architecture is tiered oversight; statutory restriction on heritable germline editing dominates at roughly eighty-two per cent; and the text-equals-practice hypothesis is empirically not supported. Next week we'll examine cross-border enforcement architectures. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The two maps chart the reconfiguration of a national gene-therapy research network between 2010 and 2024, tracking the location of central biobanks, satellite collection sites, clinical-trial centres and sample-transfer corridors.

Overall, the network expanded considerably over the period and, just as importantly, shifted from a single capital hub to a dispersed layout spanning both coasts. A system once concentrated in the east gave way to one reaching every region of the country.

In 2010, a solitary biobank in the eastern capital coordinated only three collection sites — two in the east and one in the central plain — together with a single trial centre co-located with the biobank. The transfer corridors formed a short radial pattern converging on the capital, and the western and northern regions were entirely unserved.

By 2024, a second biobank had opened in a western tech corridor, while collection sites had tripled to nine and trial centres had increased to five, one in each region plus a southern university link. The formerly unserved north gained both a collection site and a trial centre, and a dense bi-coastal mesh of cryogenic-transport corridors, including a new international link to an overseas laboratory, now connected the whole system.

The two maps trace the transformation of a national gene-therapy research network across a fourteen-year interval, contrasting its 2010 configuration with that of 2024 in terms of biobanks, collection sites, trial centres and transfer corridors.

Overall, what is most striking is not merely that the network grew, but that its very architecture was redrawn: a tightly centralised, capital-bound system was supplanted by a dispersed, bi-coastal one in which research capacity was distributed across every region. Expansion and decentralisation thus proceeded hand in hand.

In 2010, the network radiated from a single point. A lone biobank in the eastern capital governed just three collection sites and one trial centre lodged alongside it, with short corridors converging inward. Crucially, neither the west nor the north featured at all, leaving vast tracts of the country beyond the agency's reach.

By 2024, this radial logic had been inverted. So extensive was the build-out that a second biobank had appeared in the western tech corridor, collection sites had tripled to nine and trial centres had risen to five, one per region. Were the northern extension and the new international corridor overlooked, the scale of this deliberately redundant, coast-to-coast mesh would be seriously understated.

blocks.text: Gene editing tools such as CRISPR now allow clinicians to correct the faulty sequences behind incurable hereditary conditions before a single symptom ever appears.
Stem cell research holds out the promise of regenerating damaged tissue, potentially rendering many chronic illnesses far more manageable than replicate-and-hope conventional therapies ever could.
Crops engineered to be resistant to drought and pests can be grown with far fewer chemical inputs, easing pressure on both farmers and the environment.
Therapeutic cloning, which produces tissue rather than whole organisms, could one day eliminate the chronic shortage of transplant organs and the agonising waiting lists that accompany it.
Germline editing propagates any error into every subsequent generation, meaning a single miscalculation could inflict irreversible harm long after the original patient has died.
Off-target effects in imprecise editing procedures can silently alter unintended stretches of the genome, with consequences that may not surface for years.
Widespread reliance on genetically uniform crops leaves agriculture dangerously exposed, since a single new pathogen could sweep through fields lacking the genetic diversity to resist it.
The commercialisation of biotechnology risks reducing something as intimate as a person's genetic predisposition to a marketable commodity, sold to the highest bidder.
Decades of painstaking research into the human genome have finally converged with computing power sufficient to make precise gene editing commercially viable.

The overuse of antibiotics in both medicine and agriculture has driven the rapid evolution of resistant bacterial strains, a textbook case of survival of the fittest operating under artificial pressure.
Falling costs of sequencing technology have brought genetic testing within reach of ordinary consumers, fuelling public curiosity about inherited traits and ancestry.
Persistent food-security concerns in densely populated regions have pushed governments to back genetic modification research as a means of boosting crop yields.
Successful gene therapy for previously untreatable hereditary disorders has transformed prognoses that were once a death sentence into manageable, even curable, conditions.
The rise of antibiotic-resistant superbugs threatens to undo a century of progress in modern medicine, turning routine infections back into potential killers.
Widespread adoption of genetically modified staple crops has measurably increased yields in some regions, though not without disrupting local farming practices.
Public fascination with bioethical questions surrounding cloning and editing has pushed policymakers to draft legislation far faster than would otherwise have been the case.
Regulators must grapple with how to police germline editing without stifling the legitimate therapeutic research that could cure devastating diseases.
Distinguishing between a defensible medical intervention and a step towards designer babies remains a contentious issue that scientists and ethicists have yet to resolve.
Ensuring that breakthroughs in stem cell therapy reach patients in poorer countries, rather than remaining the preserve of the wealthy, poses a persistent logistical challenge.
Preventing genetically engineered organisms from cross-breeding with wild populations and disrupting fragile ecosystems has proven far harder than early optimists anticipated.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: An international moratorium on non-therapeutic germline editing would buy scientists time to establish long-term safety before the technology is used irreversibly.
Independent ethical oversight committees, rather than commercial laboratories alone, should vet every proposed application of gene editing in humans.
Rotating antibiotic use in agriculture and enforcing stricter prescription controls in medicine could slow the emergence of resistant pathogens considerably.
Subsidising stem cell and genetic modification research for neglected tropical diseases would help ensure the benefits are not confined to wealthy nations alone.
Many members of the public regard therapeutic uses of gene editing as an unambiguous good, provided the treatment targets disease rather than cosmetic enhancement.
A vocal minority insists that any tinkering with the human genome amounts to playing God, regardless of how carefully it is regulated.
Popular sentiment towards genetically modified food has gained significant traction in some markets while remaining deeply distrusted in others.
There is widespread agreement that unchecked eugenics-style selection for supposedly desirable traits would be a moral catastrophe, even among strong supporters of medical gene therapy.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: Governments bear primary responsibility for drafting legislation that keeps pace with a field evolving far faster than the committees meant to regulate it.
Scientific bodies and research institutions must enforce rigorous ethical oversight, refusing to publish or fund work that crosses a moral threshold without proper scrutiny.
Biotechnology companies developing resistant crop varieties have a duty to disclose long-term ecological data rather than prioritising profit at the expense of transparency.
International organisations should coordinate a shared framework, since a contentious issue such as germline editing cannot be resolved by any single nation acting alone.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: Although critics warn that genetic screening could revive eugenics-like thinking, proponents counter that preventing suffering from a hereditary condition is categorically different from selecting for beauty or intelligence.

While opponents insist that using animals as guinea pigs is unnecessary given modern computer modelling, many researchers maintain that complex biological systems still cannot be fully replicated in silico.

Sceptics argue that genetically modified crops are unnatural, yet supporters note that selective breeding has altered species for millennia, making the distinction largely one of degree rather than kind.

Detractors claim that cloning research is inherently reckless, but defenders point out that therapeutic cloning for organ generation is a double-edged sword whose benefits, on balance, far outweigh the drawbacks.
As sequencing costs continue to fall, personalised medicine informed by an individual's genome is likely to become standard clinical practice within a generation.
Somatic editing for serious disease is expected to gain regulatory approval in more countries, even as germline editing for enhancement remains firmly restricted.
Scientists have made significant strides in developing crops that are simultaneously resistant to drought, pests and disease, a trend that seems set to continue as climate pressures mount.
Public debate over genetic privilege is likely to intensify as enhancement technologies mature, forcing societies to confront questions of fairness they have so far been able to postpone.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas somatic editing affects only the treated individual, germline editing is transmitted to every descendant, a distinction that fundamentally changes the ethical calculus involved.
Compared with older, blunter methods of selective breeding, modern gene editing offers a precision that makes both its therapeutic promise and its potential for misuse considerably greater.
Unlike traditional crossbreeding, which can take many generations to fix a desirable trait, targeted genetic modification can introduce the same characteristic within a single generation.
In contrast to the outright prohibition once imposed on human cloning research, stem cell therapy has gradually moved from a contentious issue to a widely accepted branch of regenerative medicine.
The well-documented case of Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, remains a frequently cited historical milestone in debates about the ethics of cloning.

Widespread cultivation of genetically modified staple crops such as insect-resistant cotton illustrates how biotechnology can be adopted at scale once ethical oversight and safety testing are satisfied.
Family case studies of children born free of a hereditary condition thanks to embryo screening are often invoked to humanise otherwise abstract policy debates.
International reporting on the global spread of antibiotic-resistant infections is regularly cited as evidence of the unintended consequences of overusing a once-reliable technology.

blocks.text: The rapid maturation of gene-editing tools such as CRISPR has reopened one of biology's oldest debates: how far should humanity go in rewriting its own genome? While some argue that such technology should be used freely to enhance human capabilities, others regard it as ethically dangerous. In my view, therapeutic editing is justifiable, but the free enhancement of the germline is not.

Those who favour permissive use tend to emphasise its therapeutic promise. Many hereditary conditions — sickle-cell anaemia, cystic fibrosis and Huntington's disease — remain otherwise incurable, so gene editing represents a genuine breakthrough for the families affected by them. Indeed, if parents could prevent a child from inheriting a devastating predisposition, refusing to do so would arguably itself be unethical. Supporters also point out that enhancement lies on a continuum with vaccines, glasses and education, all of which already improve the human condition in widely accepted ways.

Critics, however, insist that we are intervening in processes we do not fully understand. Editing the germline transmits changes to every subsequent generation, yet our knowledge of complex gene interactions remains incomplete, and any mistakes could prove irreversible. There is also a real danger of a society stratified by genetic privilege, in which wealthy families purchase enhanced traits while poorer ones are left behind. Such designer-baby scenarios could entrench existing inequalities at the biological level.

In conclusion, gene editing should be permitted for serious medical conditions, where the benefits are concrete and the risks acceptable, but tightly restricted for purely cosmetic or cognitive enhancement. Provided that ethical oversight is robust and access is equitable, biotechnology can alleviate enormous suffering; an unregulated free-for-all, by contrast, would be a moral and biological gamble.

The maturation of CRISPR-Cas9 and related platforms has revived one of bioethics' most contested questions: should humanity edit its own genome at will, or should such interventions be tightly constrained? While certain enthusiasts advocate near-unrestricted use, a substantial body of scholarship warns of profound and partly unforeseeable risks. In my assessment, therapeutic somatic editing is defensible and arguably overdue, whereas germline enhancement crosses a moral threshold that prudence demands we respect.

Defenders of permissive use marshal medically compelling arguments. So devastating are monogenic disorders such as Huntington's disease and cystic fibrosis that, where a single targeted edit could avert a lifetime of suffering, refraining from intervention seems itself ethically questionable. Furthermore, agricultural and microbial applications — drought-resistant crops, malaria-suppressing gene drives, engineered insulin — already alleviate considerable global hardship, demonstrating that genome editing can be both safe and transformative when conducted under disciplined oversight rather than commercial pressure.

By contrast, opponents stress the categorical difference between somatic and heritable interventions. Were germline edits to become routine, they would propagate irreversibly through generations whose conditions of choice we cannot possibly foresee. So intricate are gene-expression networks that off-target effects cannot, at present, be reliably excluded. Beyond this technical risk lies a deeper distributive concern: in the absence of equitable access, the commodification of enhancement could entrench a stratified society in which inherited genetic privilege compounds existing inequality and renegotiates the very meaning of human normality.

In conclusion, the responsible architecture is asymmetric rather than absolute. Therapeutic somatic editing for serious disease should be actively supported under rigorous, independent oversight; non-therapeutic germline enhancement, however, should remain firmly off-limits until international governance, long-term safety data and genuine ethical consensus catch up with the underlying biotechnology. Only such an arrangement can capture the field's curative potential while forestalling its most troubling abuses. Otherwise, the immense biomedical promise of this technology risks being eclipsed by an unaccountable strain of biological hubris.

solutions.text: PHẦN A: 1. Some conditions, such as certain heart problems, are HEREDITARY and tend to run in families across several generations. — "Hereditary" (tính từ) nghĩa là di truyền qua gen; thường đi với "disorders/disease/traits", khác với "inherited" mang nghĩa rộng hơn. 2. Doctors are increasingly able to identify a genetic PREDISPOSITION towards particular illnesses long before any symptoms appear. — "Predisposition" cần giới từ "to/towards" đi kèm ("predisposition to/towards a disease"), không dùng "for". 3. A single genetic MUTATION in one gene can be enough to trigger a serious inherited disorder. — "Mutation" là danh từ đếm được chỉ sự thay đổi trong DNA; động từ tương ứng là "mutate", không dùng "mutation" như động từ. 4. Under laboratory conditions, scientists can observe how quickly a virus is able to REPLICATE itself inside a host cell. — "Replicate" nghĩa là tự sao chép chính xác; dễ nhầm với "replace" (thay thế) nên cần chú ý phát âm và nghĩa. 5. Genetic engineers have developed wheat varieties that are more RESISTANT to drought and disease than earlier strains. — "Resistant" luôn đi với giới từ "to" ("resistant to drought/pests"), không dùng "against" hay "from". 6. Height is a physical TRAIT that is influenced by both genetic factors and childhood nutrition. — "Trait" là đặc điểm/đặc tính di truyền hoặc tính cách; thường đi với "genetic trait", "inherit a trait". 7. Hospitals in several countries now offer GENE EDITING as an experimental treatment for a small number of rare inherited conditions. — "Gene editing" viết rời khi là danh từ độc lập; chỉ thêm gạch nối khi làm tính từ ghép trước danh từ ("gene-editing technology"). 8. Many people confuse reproductive CLONING with therapeutic cloning, even though the two processes serve very different purposes. — "Cloning" là quá trình tạo ra sinh vật giống hệt về gen; cần phân biệt "reproductive cloning" và "therapeutic cloning". 9. Genetic MODIFICATION of crops is often defended on the grounds that it can improve resistance to pests. — "Modification" là danh từ chỉ sự biến đổi; viết tắt "GM" chỉ dùng cho tính từ (genetically modified), không thay thế danh từ này. 10. Historians often note that the discredited theory of EUGENICS was used to justify deeply unethical policies in the twentieth century. — "Eugenics" là danh từ số ít không đếm được, mang hàm ý tiêu cực mạnh trong lịch sử nên cần dùng cẩn trọng. 11. Some scientists have called for a MORATORIUM on certain forms of experimental gene therapy until safety guidelines are agreed internationally. — "Moratorium" nghĩa là lệnh cấm/đình chỉ tạm thời; collocation phổ biến là "call for/impose a moratorium on". 12. Researchers are studying whether STEM CELL therapy could help regenerate tissue damaged by injury or disease. — "Stem cell" là danh từ ghép không cần gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ khác ("stem cell research/therapy").

PHẦN B: 1. Band 7: Scientists can genetically modify plants to make them more resistant to disease and drought. Band 8: Advances in gene editing have made it possible to engineer crop varieties that are markedly more resistant to disease and drought than their conventional counterparts. 2. Band 7: Hereditary illnesses can be passed down from parents to their children through genes. Band 8: Hereditary disorders, rooted in genetic predisposition, can increasingly be identified and, in some cases, managed before symptoms ever emerge. 3. Band 7: Many people are concerned about the ethics of human cloning. Band 8: The prospect of human cloning continues to provoke considerable bioethical debate, not least because of the profound questions it raises about identity and consent. 4. Band 7: Editing a baby's genes before birth raises difficult ethical questions. Band 8: Germline editing of embryos is arguably one of the most contentious issues in modern science, given that any changes made would be passed on to future generations. 5. Band 7: Genetic testing allows people to find out if they have a predisposition to certain diseases. Band 8: Were genetic testing to become more widely accessible, individuals could be alerted to a hereditary predisposition long before any clinical symptoms appear. 6. Band 7: Some governments have banned certain types of genetic experiments because of safety concerns. Band 8: In light of persistent safety concerns, several governments have imposed a moratorium on certain categories of genetic research pending further international guidance. 7. Band 7: Companies that collect genetic data need to protect it carefully and use it responsibly. Band 8: Given how sensitive genetic data is, companies that gather it arguably have a fiduciary duty to safeguard it and to be transparent about how it is used. 8. Band 7: New biotechnology could help increase food production and reduce hunger. Band 8: Not only could biotechnology bolster food security through more resilient, disease-resistant crops, but it may also, some researchers argue, ease pressure on land already strained by climate change.

2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Genetically Modified (GM) Foods (Solution or Danger?)

Arguments FOR GM Foods: They are essential to alleviate global hunger by increasing crop yields; they can be engineered to be resistant to drought and pests, reducing the need for harmful chemical pesticides; they can be fortified with essential vitamins (e.g., Golden Rice).

Arguments AGAINST GM Foods: The long-term health effects on humans remain largely unknown; cross-pollination with wild plants could create uncontrollable "superweeds" and irreversibly disrupt the natural ecosystem; it places control of the global food supply into the hands of a few monopolistic biotech corporations.
Topic: Cloning and Genetic Engineering in Humans

Benefits (Medical): Gene therapy could eradicate debilitating hereditary diseases before a child is even born; therapeutic cloning could generate perfectly matched organs for transplant, eliminating waiting lists and organ rejection.

Drawbacks (Bioethics): It crosses a dangerous moral boundary by allowing humans to "play God"; the creation of "designer babies" could lead to a dystopian society where genetic privilege exacerbates existing social disparities; the technology could be weaponized or misused.
Topic: Animal Testing in Scientific Research

Arguments FOR: Using animals as guinea pigs is a "necessary evil" to ensure the safety of vital vaccines and life-saving medications before human trials; complex biological systems cannot yet be fully simulated by computer models.

Arguments AGAINST: It inflicts immense suffering on sentient organisms; technological advancements (like lab-grown human tissue and advanced computer algorithms) are rendering animal testing increasingly obsolete and unnecessary.

Cue card: Describe a scientific advance you find ethically complex. You should say: what the advance is; when you first heard about it; what its potential benefits and risks are; and explain why you find it ethically difficult.
Model Answer (≈ 276 words, Band 7.5–8.0):

The scientific advance I find most ethically vertiginous is CRISPR-Cas9 germline editing — the capacity to make heritable modifications to the human genome that will be passed down to all subsequent generations. What distinguishes germline editing from its somatic counterpart is precisely this irreversibility: we are not merely treating an individual patient but rewriting the genetic blueprint of an entire lineage.

I first became aware of the technology in November 2018, when the Chinese biophysicist He Jiankui announced he had used CRISPR to create the world's first gene-edited babies — twin girls whose CCR5 gene had been disabled, ostensibly to confer HIV resistance. The international scientific community's reaction was one of near-universal condemnation, and He was subsequently imprisoned. Yet the genie, as it were, was already out of the bottle.

The potential benefits are, frankly, staggering. Hereditary disorders like Huntington's disease, sickle-cell anaemia and cystic fibrosis could theoretically be eradicated within a single generation — sparing untold suffering. Therapeutic gene editing could also dramatically expand the donor pool for organ transplantation through xenotransplantation.

The risks, however, are equally vast. Off-target mutations could introduce unforeseen pathologies that propagate indefinitely through the germline. More troublingly, the slippery slope from disease prevention to enhancement — selecting for intelligence, height or pigmentation — could entrench a form of genetic stratification that exacerbates existing socioeconomic inequities. What we'd be creating, in essence, is a bioethical chasm between the genetically enhanced and the unedited.

What makes this so vexing for me is that I can't comfortably dismiss either side. The suffering averted is morally weighty, but so too is the precautionary principle. Were I forced to take a position, I'd advocate a strict moratorium on germline editing while permitting somatic applications.

sections.title: PART 2 — Describe a scientific advance you find ethically complex

blocks.text: Q1: Should genetic enhancement for non-medical traits ever be legalised?

I'm rather firmly against it, though I recognise the line between therapy and enhancement is philosophically slippery. The core concern is distributive justice: enhancement technologies, by their very nature, will initially be accessible only to the wealthy, which means we'd be hard-coding existing socioeconomic disparities into the human genome itself. What philosopher Michael Sandel has termed "the case against perfection" resonates with me here — there's something corrosive about treating children as bespoke products rather than gifts to be welcomed unconditionally. That said, I acknowledge the regulatory challenge: even if one jurisdiction bans enhancement, reproductive tourism to permissive countries would inevitably emerge. So a robust international framework — analogous perhaps to the Biological Weapons Convention — would be necessary. Until such governance exists, and arguably even afterwards, I'd maintain that we shouldn't be tinkering with the heritable germline for cosmetic or competitive purposes. The risks of a stratified post-human society are simply too dystopian.
Q2: Who should own genetic data — individuals, corporations, or the state?

This is genuinely one of the defining questions of biotech governance, and I'd argue strongly for individual ownership with strict fiduciary obligations on custodians. The current landscape is rather alarming: companies like 23andMe have built databases of millions of genomes, and their commercial partnerships with pharmaceutical giants have raised legitimate concerns about consent drift — the gradual repurposing of data beyond the original authorisation. What I find particularly troubling is that genetic data is intrinsically familial; sharing your genome implicates the privacy of your siblings, parents and unborn descendants in ways traditional consent frameworks struggle to accommodate. The 23andMe data breach affecting nearly 7 million users in 2023 underscored the catastrophic stakes. My preferred model would treat genetic data as inalienable personal property, with companies operating as data trustees subject to GDPR-style rights of erasure and portability. State ownership, conversely, I find genuinely Orwellian.
Q3: Can biotechnology realistically solve global hunger?

I'm cautiously optimistic, though I think it's only part of the solution. The case for biotech-enabled food security is compelling: drought-resistant CRISPR-edited crops, Golden Rice fortified with vitamin A, and nitrogen-fixing cereals could meaningfully boost yields in climate-stressed regions. Indeed, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation has channelled hundreds of millions into precisely these initiatives, with promising results in sub-Saharan Africa. That said, framing hunger as primarily a production problem misses the structural reality. The World Food Programme has consistently documented that global agriculture already produces enough calories to feed roughly 10 billion people; the issue is distribution, conflict, food waste and purchasing power, not raw output. So biotech can certainly contribute, but expecting it to single-handedly solve hunger is, I think, naively techno-optimistic. The deeper fix requires confronting agricultural subsidies, trade asymmetries and the political economy of food sovereignty — which no genome editor can resolve.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Welcome back. Today's lecture engages three deeply contested questions in contemporary bioethics: CRISPR ethics, germline editing and the institutional role of bioethics committees. The temptation to frame gene editing as merely a technical advance, I will argue, evades the underlying moral architecture.

> Let us begin with CRISPR-Cas9 ethics. The 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier for engineering a programmable enzyme that cuts DNA at precisely targeted sequences. Somatic editing — confined to a single patient's non-reproductive cells — is widely regarded as ethically continuous with conventional gene therapy. The first somatic CRISPR therapy, Casgevy for sickle-cell disease, received regulatory approval in 2023. So far, so consensual.

> Now, germline editing. Edits to embryos, eggs or sperm propagate heritably through every subsequent generation. In 2018, the Chinese biophysicist He Jiankui announced the birth of twin girls whose embryos he had edited to confer HIV resistance — the so-called CCR5 edit. The international scientific community responded with near-universal condemnation; He was subsequently sentenced to three years in prison. A 2019 commentary in Nature, signed by eighteen scientists across seven countries, called for a global moratorium on heritable human genome editing.

> Finally, bioethics committees. Bodies such as the UK's Nuffield Council on Bioethics and the US Presidential Commission for the Study of Bioethical Issues offer deliberative scaffolding, but they are advisory, not binding. Their legitimacy depends on procedural inclusion of patients, religious communities and disability-rights advocates — voices too often marginalised in expert-only forums.

Now, before we treat that somatic-germline boundary as a comfortable firewall, let me trouble it a little, because the science has a way of eroding the very lines our ethics depends on. Take mitochondrial replacement therapy — so-called three-parent IVF, legalised in the United Kingdom back in 2015. Strictly speaking, it edits the germline: the swapped mitochondrial DNA is heritable down the maternal line. Yet because it targets a tiny, non-nuclear genome and aims only to prevent devastating mitochondrial disease, regulators carved out an exception. [pause] Um, and that single exception tells you something important — namely that "germline editing" is not one moral object but a spectrum, and the location of the permissible threshold is being negotiated case by case, quietly, in committee rooms.

Let me introduce a distinction the He Jiankui scandal rather overshadowed: the difference between therapy and enhancement. Correcting a single-gene disorder like Huntington's commands broad sympathy. But the same toolkit could, in principle, be turned toward polygenic traits — height, say, or cognitive tendencies — where the science is flimsy and the social risks acute. The bioethicist might call this the slippery-slope worry, and ordinarily I'm wary of slippery-slope arguments. Here, though, the slope is greased by a real market incentive: fertility clinics competing on what they can offer prospective parents.

There's also a justice dimension I think we neglect at our peril. Casgevy, that pioneering sickle-cell therapy, carries a list price north of two million dollars per patient. Well, consider the irony — sickle-cell disease burdens populations in sub-Saharan Africa most heavily, precisely the regions least able to afford a cure priced like a luxury asset. [pause] So even a flawlessly ethical somatic edit can entrench, rather than dissolve, global health inequity. Which forces the question of who governs access, who governs the germline threshold, and through what binding instruments rather than mere advisory ones — and it is to those regulatory architectures that I now want to turn…

> The synthesis is humbling: the technical capacity now outruns our deliberative bandwidth. Caution, here, is not timidity but prudence. Now, please consult table two, which catalogues national germline-editing regulations…

In 2010, a solitary biobank in the eastern capital coordinated only three collection sites — two in the east and one in the central plain — together with a single trial centre co-located with the biobank. The transfer corridors formed a short radial pattern converging on the capital, and the western and northern regions were entirely unserved.

By 2024, a second biobank had opened in a western tech corridor, while collection sites had tripled to nine and trial centres had increased to five, one in each region plus a southern university link. The formerly unserved north gained both a collection site and a trial centre, and a dense bi-coastal mesh of cryogenic-transport corridors, including a new international link to an overseas laboratory, now connected the whole system.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~198 từ)

The two maps trace the transformation of a national gene-therapy research network across a fourteen-year interval, contrasting its 2010 configuration with that of 2024 in terms of biobanks, collection sites, trial centres and transfer corridors.

Overall, what is most striking is not merely that the network grew, but that its very architecture was redrawn: a tightly centralised, capital-bound system was supplanted by a dispersed, bi-coastal one in which research capacity was distributed across every region. Expansion and decentralisation thus proceeded hand in hand.

In 2010, the network radiated from a single point. A lone biobank in the eastern capital governed just three collection sites and one trial centre lodged alongside it, with short corridors converging inward. Crucially, neither the west nor the north featured at all, leaving vast tracts of the country beyond the agency's reach.

By 2024, this radial logic had been inverted. So extensive was the build-out that a second biobank had appeared in the western tech corridor, collection sites had tripled to nine and trial centres had risen to five, one per region. Were the northern extension and the new international corridor overlooked, the scale of this deliberately redundant, coast-to-coast mesh would be seriously understated.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 viết Overview ở tầng khái quát cao hơn — không chỉ nói 'mở rộng' mà nhận định 'kiến trúc mạng lưới bị vẽ lại' (centralised bị thay bằng dispersed/bi-coastal), thể hiện Task Achievement vượt trội so với Band 7.

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp dày hơn: đảo ngữ ('So extensive was the build-out that ...'), câu điều kiện đảo ('Were the northern extension ... overlooked ...') và bị động học thuật ('was supplanted by', 'had been inverted'), trong khi Band 7 chủ yếu dùng 'gave way to' và past perfect đơn giản.

•  Band 8 chọn từ chính xác và sang hơn ('radiated from a single point', 'radial logic had been inverted', 'deliberately redundant, coast-to-coast mesh') và liên kết mượt hơn, nâng cả Lexical Resource lẫn Coherence một bậc.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)

•  Đọc cả hai bản đồ trong 30 giây để chốt 'mỏ neo' cho Overview: (1) mạng lưới mở rộng về số lượng cơ sở, (2) bố cục chuyển từ một trung tâm thủ đô sang trải đều nhiều vùng — đây là khung cho toàn bài.
•  Viết Overview chỉ bằng hai ý xu hướng (mở rộng + phi tập trung hoá), TUYỆT ĐỐI không nêu con số cụ thể; để số liệu cho hai đoạn thân bài.
•  Tổ chức thân bài theo trục thời gian: một đoạn cho hiện trạng 2010 (dùng quá khứ đơn), một đoạn cho 2024 kèm so sánh (dùng past perfect 'had tripled / had opened').

•  Dùng lexis bản đồ chuyên biệt: 'co-located with', 'radial pattern', 'bi-coastal mesh', 'formerly unserved', 'cryogenic-transport corridor' để nâng Lexical Resource thay vì lặp 'in the north / in the south'.
•  Khép bài bằng một chi tiết tổng kết có sức nặng (vùng bắc được phủ + hành lang quốc tế mới) thể hiện so sánh, thay vì liệt kê rời rạc từng ký hiệu trên bản đồ.

(1) Đề bài
Đề bài.  Some people argue that gene editing should be used freely to enhance human capabilities, while others see it as ethically dangerous. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
(2) Từ vựng chủ đề (Band 8 topic & argument lexis)

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
Phía ủng hộ dùng tự do (nhấn lợi ích chữa bệnh & tiến bộ):
•  Nhiều bệnh di truyền nan y (xơ nang, thiếu máu hồng cầu hình liềm, Huntington) có thể được ngăn chặn ngay từ gốc.
•  Nếu cha mẹ có thể loại bỏ một khuynh hướng bệnh tàn khốc cho con mà từ chối làm thì bản thân điều đó cũng đáng bị chất vấn về đạo đức.
•  Chỉnh sửa gen nằm trên cùng một mạch tiến bộ với vắc-xin, kính mắt và giáo dục — đều 'nâng cấp' điều kiện con người.
Phía cảnh báo nguy hiểm đạo đức (nhấn rủi ro & bất bình đẳng):
•  Chỉnh sửa dòng mầm truyền thay đổi sang mọi thế hệ sau trong khi hiểu biết về tương tác gen vẫn chưa đầy đủ, sai sót khó đảo ngược.
•  Nguy cơ một xã hội phân tầng theo 'đặc quyền di truyền', nơi nhà giàu mua được đặc điểm ưu việt còn người nghèo bị bỏ lại.
•  Ranh giới giữa chữa bệnh và nâng cấp thẩm mỹ/nhận thức rất mờ, dễ trượt sang lạm dụng nếu không có giám sát chặt.
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion
•  Introduction — diễn giải tranh luận về việc chỉnh sửa gen để nâng cấp con người; thesis: ủng hộ ứng dụng chữa bệnh có giám sát nhưng phản đối nâng cấp dòng mầm không thiết yếu.
•  Body 1 — vì sao nhiều người ủng hộ: tiềm năng chữa bệnh di truyền nan y, lập luận đạo đức về việc 'từ chối cứu cũng là vô đạo', và tính liên tục với các tiến bộ y học khác.
•  Body 2 — vì sao nhiều người lo ngại: rủi ro không thể đảo ngược của chỉnh sửa dòng mầm, nguy cơ bất bình đẳng/đặc quyền di truyền, ranh giới chữa bệnh–nâng cấp mờ nhạt.
•  Conclusion — quan điểm cân bằng: cho phép chỉnh sửa chữa bệnh với giám sát đạo đức nghiêm ngặt, nhưng hạn chế chặt nâng cấp dòng mầm cho tới khi có đồng thuận và dữ liệu an toàn.
(5) Mẫu câu luyện tập (Practice sentences)

rows: Câu thesis có lập trường rõ + phân biệt phạm vi
While I accept that therapeutic gene editing is not only permissible but arguably overdue, I regard the free use of germline enhancement as an ethical step too far.
Phân biệt rạch ròi 'therapeutic' (đồng tình) và 'enhancement' (phản đối) ngay ở thesis.
Câu nhấn lợi ích bằng cleft
It is the prospect of eradicating incurable hereditary conditions that lends the permissive case its genuine moral force.
Dùng cleft 'It is ... that' để nhấn luận điểm trung tâm.
Câu phản biện về dòng mầm (đảo ngữ điều kiện)
Were germline edits to become routine, they would propagate irreversibly through future generations made under conditions of incomplete knowledge.
Đảo ngữ 'Were ... to become' thay cho 'If ... became'.
Câu nêu rủi ro bất bình đẳng (nominalisation)
The commodification of genetic enhancement could entrench a stratified society in which inherited privilege is encoded at the biological level.
Dùng danh hoá 'the commodification of ...' để nâng register.
Câu kết tổng hợp cân bằng

I therefore favour an asymmetric policy: therapeutic editing should be supported under rigorous oversight, whereas enhancement of the germline should remain off-limits until safety and consensus mature.
Kết hợp ủng hộ có điều kiện + giới hạn rõ ràng ('asymmetric policy').

"crossing a threshold beyond which the changes become difficult to contain or reverse"

"The genie is out of the bottle"

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~280 words)

The rapid maturation of gene-editing tools such as CRISPR has reopened one of biology's oldest debates: how far should humanity go in rewriting its own genome? While some argue that such technology should be used freely to enhance human capabilities, others regard it as ethically dangerous. In my view, therapeutic editing is justifiable, but the free enhancement of the germline is not.

Those who favour permissive use tend to emphasise its therapeutic promise. Many hereditary conditions — sickle-cell anaemia, cystic fibrosis and Huntington's disease — remain otherwise incurable, so gene editing represents a genuine breakthrough for the families affected by them. Indeed, if parents could prevent a child from inheriting a devastating predisposition, refusing to do so would arguably itself be unethical. Supporters also point out that enhancement lies on a continuum with vaccines, glasses and education, all of which already improve the human condition in widely accepted ways.

Critics, however, insist that we are intervening in processes we do not fully understand. Editing the germline transmits changes to every subsequent generation, yet our knowledge of complex gene interactions remains incomplete, and any mistakes could prove irreversible. There is also a real danger of a society stratified by genetic privilege, in which wealthy families purchase enhanced traits while poorer ones are left behind. Such designer-baby scenarios could entrench existing inequalities at the biological level.

In conclusion, gene editing should be permitted for serious medical conditions, where the benefits are concrete and the risks acceptable, but tightly restricted for purely cosmetic or cognitive enhancement. Provided that ethical oversight is robust and access is equitable, biotechnology can alleviate enormous suffering; an unregulated free-for-all, by contrast, would be a moral and biological gamble.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~316 words)

The maturation of CRISPR-Cas9 and related platforms has revived one of bioethics' most contested questions: should humanity edit its own genome at will, or should such interventions be tightly constrained? While certain enthusiasts advocate near-unrestricted use, a substantial body of scholarship warns of profound and partly unforeseeable risks. In my assessment, therapeutic somatic editing is defensible and arguably overdue, whereas germline enhancement crosses a moral threshold that prudence demands we respect.

Defenders of permissive use marshal medically compelling arguments. So devastating are monogenic disorders such as Huntington's disease and cystic fibrosis that, where a single targeted edit could avert a lifetime of suffering, refraining from intervention seems itself ethically questionable. Furthermore, agricultural and microbial applications — drought-resistant crops, malaria-suppressing gene drives, engineered insulin — already alleviate considerable global hardship, demonstrating that genome editing can be both safe and transformative when conducted under disciplined oversight rather than commercial pressure.

By contrast, opponents stress the categorical difference between somatic and heritable interventions. Were germline edits to become routine, they would propagate irreversibly through generations whose conditions of choice we cannot possibly foresee. So intricate are gene-expression networks that off-target effects cannot, at present, be reliably excluded. Beyond this technical risk lies a deeper distributive concern: in the absence of equitable access, the commodification of enhancement could entrench a stratified society in which inherited genetic privilege compounds existing inequality and renegotiates the very meaning of human normality.

In conclusion, the responsible architecture is asymmetric rather than absolute. Therapeutic somatic editing for serious disease should be actively supported under rigorous, independent oversight; non-therapeutic germline enhancement, however, should remain firmly off-limits until international governance, long-term safety data and genuine ethical consensus catch up with the underlying biotechnology. Only such an arrangement can capture the field's curative potential while forestalling its most troubling abuses. Otherwise, the immense biomedical promise of this technology risks being eclipsed by an unaccountable strain of biological hubris.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp dày đặc và chính xác hơn: đảo ngữ ('So devastating are monogenic disorders ... that ...'), điều kiện đảo ('Were germline edits to become routine ...') và danh hoá ('the commodification of enhancement', 'the responsible architecture is asymmetric'), trong khi Band 7 chủ yếu dùng câu phức thường và một mệnh đề điều kiện.

•  Band 8 nâng lexis lên bậc chuyên ngành ('somatic vs germline editing', 'monogenic disorders', 'off-target', 'biological hubris', 'distributive concern') và giữ register đạo đức-sinh học nhất quán, thay cho cụm hơi đời thường ở Band 7 như 'free-for-all', 'moral and biological gamble'.

•  Band 8 lập luận sắc hơn ở phần phản biện — phân biệt rõ rủi ro kỹ thuật (off-target, không đảo ngược) với rủi ro phân phối (bất bình đẳng) — và kết bài bằng 'asymmetric architecture' mạch lạc, nâng Coherence & Task Response một bậc so với kết bài gọn nhưng phẳng hơn của Band 7.

vocabulary.definition_en: the complete set of genetic material present in a cell or organism
vocabulary.definition_vi: bộ gen, hệ gen (toàn bộ vật chất di truyền)

Gốc Latin "mutare" (thay đổi) → mutation = một sự thay đổi trong mã di truyền.

> Editing the human genome raises profound **bioethical** questions that society has yet to resolve.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"bio-" (sinh học) + "ethical" (đạo đức) → những vấn đề đạo đức nảy sinh từ khoa học sự sống.

vocabulary.memory_hook: 'trait' nghe gần 'trace' (dấu vết) → một đặc điểm để lại 'dấu vết' nhận dạng của một cá thể hay loài.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chỉnh sửa gen, thay đổi chính xác DNA bằng công nghệ sinh học như CRISPR.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Advances in **gene editing** have opened up unprecedented therapeutic possibilities for treating inherited diseases.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"gene" (gen) + "editing" (biên tập, chỉnh sửa) → chỉnh sửa trực tiếp vào mã di truyền như sửa văn bản.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi dùng làm tính từ ghép trước danh từ cần gạch nối: 'gene-editing technology'; khi là danh từ độc lập thì viết rời 'gene editing'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of making precise changes to an organism's DNA using biotechnology tools such as CRISPR
vocabulary.definition_vi: chỉnh sửa gen (bằng công nghệ như CRISPR)
vocabulary.example: Advances in gene editing have opened up unprecedented therapeutic possibilities for treating inherited diseases.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'gene' (gen) + 'editing' (biên tập, chỉnh sửa) → chỉnh sửa trực tiếp vào mã di truyền như sửa văn bản.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự nhân bản, tạo ra sinh vật giống hệt về mặt di truyền bằng công nghệ sinh học.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Therapeutic **cloning** could one day allow doctors to grow replacement organs from a patient's own cells.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"clone" (bản sao) + "-ing" → quá trình tạo ra những bản sao giống hệt về mặt di truyền.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'therapeutic cloning' (nhân bản để chữa bệnh, không tạo sinh vật hoàn chỉnh) với 'reproductive cloning' (nhân bản tạo ra cá thể mới hoàn chỉnh).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of producing an organism that is genetically identical to another, using biotechnology
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự nhân bản (tạo ra sinh vật giống hệt về gen)
vocabulary.example: Therapeutic cloning could one day allow doctors to grow replacement organs from a patient's own cells.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'clone' (bản sao) + '-ing' → quá trình tạo ra những bản sao giống hệt về mặt di truyền.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đạo đức sinh học, ngành nghiên cứu các vấn đề đạo đức trong y sinh học.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Questions of **bioethics** have become impossible to ignore since the first gene-edited babies were announced in 2018.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"bio-" (sự sống) + "ethics" (đạo đức) → ngành nghiên cứu đạo đức liên quan đến sự sống và y học.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Bioethics' là danh từ số ít không đếm được dù có tận cùng '-s', giống như 'ethics', 'physics'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the branch of ethics concerned with the moral issues arising from advances in biology, medicine, and biotechnology
vocabulary.definition_vi: đạo đức sinh học (ngành nghiên cứu đạo đức trong y sinh)
vocabulary.example: Questions of bioethics have become impossible to ignore since the first gene-edited babies were announced in 2018.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'bio-' (sự sống) + 'ethics' (đạo đức) → ngành nghiên cứu đạo đức liên quan đến sự sống và y học.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự biến đổi, cải biến, đặc biệt về mặt cấu trúc di truyền.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Genetic **modification** can bolster food security, though not without ecological risk.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"modify" (biến đổi) + "-ication" → danh từ chỉ quá trình hoặc kết quả của việc biến đổi.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết tắt phổ biến 'GM' (genetically modified) chỉ dùng cho tính từ, không thay thế được danh từ 'modification'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the act or process of changing something, especially the genetic structure of an organism
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự biến đổi, cải biến (đặc biệt về mặt di truyền)
vocabulary.example: Genetic modification can bolster food security, though not without ecological risk.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'modify' (biến đổi) + '-ication' → danh từ chỉ quá trình hoặc kết quả của việc biến đổi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuyết ưu sinh, quan điểm gây tranh cãi về việc chọn lọc di truyền để cải thiện giống người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The spectre of **eugenics** looms over debates about selecting for desirable genetic traits in embryos.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Hy Lạp "eu-" (tốt) + "genos" (nòi giống) → ý tưởng gây tranh cãi về việc tạo ra nòi giống "tốt hơn".
vocabulary.common_error: 'Eugenics' là danh từ số ít không đếm được; mang hàm ý tiêu cực mạnh trong lịch sử, nên tránh dùng nhẹ nhàng hoặc trung lập.
vocabulary.definition_en: the discredited practice or belief of improving the genetic quality of a human population by selective breeding
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuyết ưu sinh (lựa chọn di truyền để 'cải thiện' giống người)
vocabulary.example: The spectre of eugenics looms over debates about selecting for desirable genetic traits in embryos.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Hy Lạp 'eu-' (tốt) + 'genos' (nòi giống) → ý tưởng gây tranh cãi về việc tạo ra nòi giống 'tốt hơn'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chỉnh sửa dòng mầm, tác động lên tế bào sinh dục nên di truyền cho các thế hệ sau.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Germline editing** propagates heritably through every subsequent generation, raising intergenerational ethical stakes.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"germ" (mầm, ở đây nghĩa tế bào sinh dục) + "line" (dòng) → chỉnh sửa vào "dòng mầm" nên di truyền cho con cháu.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt với 'somatic editing' (chỉ ảnh hưởng đến một cá thể, không di truyền); nhầm lẫn hai khái niệm này là lỗi phổ biến.
vocabulary.definition_en: genetic editing of reproductive cells or embryos, such that the changes are heritable and passed to future generations
vocabulary.definition_vi: chỉnh sửa dòng mầm (di truyền được cho thế hệ sau)
vocabulary.example: Germline editing propagates heritably through every subsequent generation, raising intergenerational ethical stakes.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'germ' (mầm, ở đây nghĩa tế bào sinh dục) + 'line' (dòng) → chỉnh sửa vào 'dòng mầm' nên di truyền cho con cháu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vượt trội hơn hẳn so với những mặt hạn chế hoặc bất lợi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Proponents argue that the medical benefits of gene therapy **far outweigh the drawbacks** of its high cost.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"out-" (vượt) + "weigh" (cân nặng) → lợi ích "nặng hơn" hẳn so với mặt hạn chế.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Outweigh' là động từ nguyên thể không thêm giới từ đi kèm ('outweigh sth'), không dùng 'outweigh than' hay 'outweigh over'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be much greater in importance or value than the disadvantages
vocabulary.definition_vi: vượt trội hơn hẳn so với những mặt hạn chế
vocabulary.example: Proponents argue that the medical benefits of gene therapy far outweigh the drawbacks of its high cost.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'out-' (vượt) + 'weigh' (cân nặng) → lợi ích 'nặng hơn' hẳn so với mặt hạn chế.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vấn đề gây tranh cãi, dễ dẫn đến bất đồng quan điểm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Human germline editing remains **a highly contentious issue** among scientists, ethicists and policymakers alike.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"contend" (tranh luận) + "-ious" → một vấn đề khiến người ta tranh luận gay gắt.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'contentious' (gây tranh cãi) với 'contentious' phát âm sai giống 'contented' (hài lòng) — nghĩa hoàn toàn trái ngược.
vocabulary.definition_en: a subject or topic that is likely to cause disagreement or controversy
vocabulary.definition_vi: vấn đề gây tranh cãi
vocabulary.example: Human germline editing remains a highly contentious issue among scientists, ethicists and policymakers alike.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'contend' (tranh luận) + '-ious' → một vấn đề khiến người ta tranh luận gay gắt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bản sao y hệt, giống hệt người hoặc vật khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He looks exactly like his father; he's a **carbon copy** of him in every way.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"carbon paper" xưa dùng để tạo bản sao giấy giống hệt bản gốc → "carbon copy" = bản sao giống hệt.
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ luôn cần giới từ 'of' khi nêu người được so sánh: 'a carbon copy of his father'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person or thing that closely resembles another, as if an exact duplicate
vocabulary.definition_vi: bản sao y hệt, giống hệt (người/vật khác)
vocabulary.example: He looks exactly like his father; he's a carbon copy of him in every way.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'carbon paper' xưa dùng để tạo bản sao giấy giống hệt bản gốc → 'carbon copy' = bản sao giống hệt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trong máu, bẩm sinh, mang tính di truyền về tài năng hay tính cách.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Racing **is in his blood**; both his father and grandfather were professional drivers.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Máu ("blood") mang gen di truyền → tài năng hay tính cách "nằm trong máu" là bẩm sinh, di truyền.
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ dùng với sở hữu cách 'in one's blood', không dùng mạo từ 'a/the' trước 'blood'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be a natural or inherited part of someone's character or ability
vocabulary.definition_vi: trong máu, bẩm sinh (đặc điểm/tài năng)
vocabulary.example: Racing is in his blood; both his father and grandfather were professional drivers.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Máu ('blood') mang gen di truyền → tài năng hay tính cách 'nằm trong máu' là bẩm sinh, di truyền.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phá vỡ khuôn mẫu cũ, tạo ra điều hoàn toàn mới và khác biệt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> This new gene-editing technique **breaks the mould**, offering a radically different approach to treating inherited disease.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"mould" (khuôn đúc) → "break the mould" = đập vỡ khuôn cũ để tạo ra thứ hoàn toàn mới.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh là 'mould', không phải 'mold' (Anh-Mỹ); nghĩa bóng không liên quan đến nấm mốc.
vocabulary.definition_en: to do something in a completely new and different way, breaking from tradition
vocabulary.definition_vi: phá vỡ khuôn mẫu, tạo ra điều hoàn toàn mới
vocabulary.example: This new gene-editing technique breaks the mould, offering a radically different approach to treating inherited disease.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'mould' (khuôn đúc) → 'break the mould' = đập vỡ khuôn cũ để tạo ra thứ hoàn toàn mới.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự sinh tồn của kẻ thích nghi nhất, nguyên lý cốt lõi của chọn lọc tự nhiên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Survival of the fittest** ensures that only the best-adapted organisms pass on their genes to the next generation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"survival" (sự sống sót) + "fittest" (thích nghi nhất) → không phải kẻ mạnh nhất mà là kẻ thích nghi tốt nhất mới tồn tại.
collocations: a classic case of survival of the fittest
natural selection and survival of the fittest
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là cụm cố định từ thuyết Darwin, không đổi 'fittest' thành 'strongest' dù hay bị hiểu nhầm là 'kẻ mạnh nhất'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the principle that organisms best adapted to their environment are most likely to survive and reproduce
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự sinh tồn của kẻ thích nghi nhất (thuyết chọn lọc tự nhiên)
vocabulary.example: Survival of the fittest ensures that only the best-adapted organisms pass on their genes to the next generation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'survival' (sự sống sót) + 'fittest' (thích nghi nhất) → không phải kẻ mạnh nhất mà là kẻ thích nghi tốt nhất mới tồn tại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vật thí nghiệm, người hoặc vật được đem ra thử nghiệm khoa học.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Volunteers who acted as **guinea pigs** for the experimental vaccine trial were closely monitored for side effects.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Chuột lang ("guinea pig") là loài vật thường dùng trong thí nghiệm khoa học → nghĩa bóng chỉ "người/vật bị đem ra thử nghiệm".
collocations: use sb as a guinea pig
vocabulary.common_error: Không viết hoa 'guinea pig' khi dùng nghĩa bóng (vật thí nghiệm); phân biệt với loài vật thật (chuột lang).
vocabulary.definition_en: a person or thing used as the subject of an experiment, especially in medical or scientific testing
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật thí nghiệm, người/vật được đem ra thử nghiệm
vocabulary.example: Volunteers who acted as guinea pigs for the experimental vaccine trial were closely monitored for side effects.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Chuột lang ('guinea pig') là loài vật thường dùng trong thí nghiệm khoa học → nghĩa bóng chỉ 'người/vật bị đem ra thử nghiệm'.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đóng vai thần thánh, can thiệp vượt quá giới hạn tự nhiên vào sự sống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Critics argue that designer-baby technology amounts to **playing God** with human life.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"play" (đóng vai) + "God" (Thượng đế) → con người tự cho mình quyền quyết định sự sống như thần thánh.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn viết hoa 'God' trong thành ngữ này dù không phải đang nói về tôn giáo cụ thể.
vocabulary.definition_en: to act as if one has unlimited power or authority, especially by making decisions that affect life, death, or nature
vocabulary.definition_vi: đóng vai thần thánh, can thiệp vượt quá giới hạn tự nhiên
vocabulary.example: Critics argue that designer-baby technology amounts to playing God with human life.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'play' (đóng vai) + 'God' (Thượng đế) → con người tự cho mình quyền quyết định sự sống như thần thánh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tế bào gốc, có khả năng biệt hoá thành nhiều loại tế bào khác nhau trong cơ thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Stem cell** research could revolutionise medicine by enabling doctors to regenerate damaged tissue.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"stem" (gốc, thân) + "cell" (tế bào) → tế bào "gốc" có thể phát triển thành nhiều loại tế bào khác.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi làm tính từ ghép trước danh từ, không cần gạch nối: 'stem cell research', khác với một số cụm ghép khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: an undifferentiated cell capable of developing into many different cell types in the body
vocabulary.definition_vi: tế bào gốc (có thể biệt hoá thành nhiều loại tế bào khác nhau)
vocabulary.example: Stem cell research could revolutionise medicine by enabling doctors to regenerate damaged tissue.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'stem' (gốc, thân) + 'cell' (tế bào) → tế bào 'gốc' có thể phát triển thành nhiều loại tế bào khác.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Lệnh cấm hoặc đình chỉ tạm thời một hoạt động, chờ giải quyết vấn đề.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many scientists called for a global **moratorium** on human germline editing following the 2018 controversy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin "mora" (sự trì hoãn) → moratorium = lệnh tạm dừng, trì hoãn một hoạt động.
vocabulary.common_error: Số nhiều chuẩn học thuật là 'moratoria', dù 'moratoriums' cũng được chấp nhận trong văn phong ít trang trọng hơn.
vocabulary.definition_en: a temporary official ban or suspension of an activity, typically imposed until an issue is resolved
vocabulary.definition_vi: lệnh cấm/đình chỉ tạm thời (chờ giải quyết vấn đề)
vocabulary.example: Many scientists called for a global moratorium on human germline editing following the 2018 controversy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Latin 'mora' (sự trì hoãn) → moratorium = lệnh tạm dừng, trì hoãn một hoạt động.
